title: Alveolar Echinococcosis in Children
case_text:
A 14-month-old boy (height 78 cm, weight 8 kg) with a history of Down syndrome, corrected tetralogy of Fallot, generalized epilepsy, and failure to thrive was accidentally diagnosed with a 4 mm sized cyst in the spleen during further investigation because of unsuccessful treatment of pneumonia. The cyst posed a suspicion of echinococcosis and both E. multilocularis and E. granulosus IgG antibodies were found to be positive: 0.231 optical density (OD) (cut-off 0.16) and 1.338 OD (cut-off 0.899), respectively. To verify the diagnosis in a few days the tests were repeated and E. granulosus IgG was found to be negative while Western blot confirmed positive IgG against E. multilocularis. The diagnosis of AE was confirmed and treatment with albendazole (ABZ) powder 10 mg/kg/day divided in two doses was prescribed.
The patient was followed up every three months repeating abdominal ultrasound (US) and testing hepatic enzymes. During the course of the patient's follow-up no changes were seen: the size of the cyst remained the same (4 x 2.5 mm-3.9 x 2.7 mm), hepatic enzymes always remained within a normal range, and E. multilocularis IgG persisted to be positive:1.072 (OD) (cut-off 0.473). The patient was discussed with surgeons and it was decided that no intervention was indicated because of the small size of the cyst; thus the follow-up of the patient was continued. After 1 year, the treatment with ABZ was temporarily suspended because the patient underwent heart surgery for the tetralogy of Fallot. At that time in the place of cyst only hyperechogenic zone was found. However, three months later a 4 mm sized cyst in the same place with clear fluid and narrow borders was found again and treatment with ABZ 10 mg/kg/day was reinitiated.
On the last examination (after 1 year and 8 months of treatment) no positive changes were seen: E. multilocularis IgG remained high (1.75 (OD), cut-off 0.99) and the cyst was of the same size; however, no new foci were detected. The boy tolerates the medication well and is continued to be followed up every three months.

   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: splenic alveolar echinococcosis
